us2_founding.topic: Founding documents and structure: US Constitution (Article V, Tenth Amendment, federalism) vs Israel's Basic Laws (count, entrenchment, Torah Study 2026), unitary local government

claims.text: US Constitution Article V: amendments proposed by two-thirds of both Houses (or a convention called on application of two-thirds of state legislatures) and ratified by three-fourths of the states; 27 amendments, the last in 1992
Tenth Amendment (1791): 'The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.'

Basic Law: Freedom of Occupation s.7: 'shall not be varied except by a Basic Law passed by a majority of the members of the Knesset'; s.8 override: a law violating it has effect if passed by a majority of MKs, expressly states so, and expires after four years

Basic Laws list: The Knesset 1958 (s.4 electoral system amendable only by 61 MKs), Israel Lands 1960, President 1964, Government 1968/1992/2001, State Economy 1975, Military 1976, Jerusalem 1980, Judiciary 1984, State Comptroller 1988, Human Dignity and Liberty 1992 (32-21), Freedom of Occupation 1994, Referendum 2014, Nation-State 2018, Torah Study 2026; Bank Mizrahi (1995) held laws violating limitation clauses void

Basic Law: Torah Study passed 13 July 2026 by 63-52; declares Torah study a 'foundational value'; Movement for Quality Government petitioned the High Court immediately, calling the package 'a draft exemption law through the back door'; Likud's Edelstein and Illouz voted against; Netanyahu absent

Israel is a unitary country with one level of subnational government: 258 local authorities in 2021 (76 municipalities, 126 local councils, 56 regional councils); subnational spending 12.8% of public expenditure and 5.9% of GDP (2020); grants 54.0% and taxes 39.7% of subnational revenue; council bylaws and budgets subject to Interior Ministry approval
OECD: Israeli local governments are funded mainly by central-government grants and the arnona property tax, levied by physical size rather than value
